Chapter 2: Setting Up Your Workshop: Environment Setup
Every great project starts with a well-organized workshop. For DevAgentZero, this means setting up your computer with the right tools and folder structure. A meticulously prepared and standardized local environment is not just a preliminary step; it is the first layer of resilience for the agent. The self-healing systems we will build in the next chapter rely on a predictable and stable baseline to function correctly. By following these steps, you are building the agent's stable "home," dramatically increasing the chances of a successful build.1
2.1 Hardware and Software Prerequisites
DevAgentZero is designed to run on a modern personal computer. While it is highly optimized, running Large Language Models locally requires a decent amount of system resources. Here are the recommended specifications 1:
Operating System: Windows 11 is used for this guide, but the instructions are easily adaptable for macOS and Linux.
RAM: 16 GB is the minimum, but 32 GB is recommended for smoother performance when running larger models.
Disk Space: A minimum of 90 GB of free space on your primary drive is recommended to accommodate the agent, its memory logs, and multiple LLM models.
Processor: A modern multi-core processor (e.g., Intel i7 12th-gen or equivalent) is ideal.
2.2 Installing Python and Essential Libraries
The agent is written in Python, so the first step is to ensure you have the correct version installed.
Install Python 3.11+:
Navigate to the official Python downloads page for Windows.
Download the installer for the latest version of Python 3.11 or higher.
Run the installer. Crucially, on the first screen of the installation, make sure to check the box that says "Add Python to PATH." This allows you to run Python from any terminal window.
To verify the installation, open a new Command Prompt or PowerShell window and type python --version. It should display the version you just installed.1
Install Required Libraries:
DevAgentZero relies on several third-party Python libraries to function. These libraries provide tools for everything from displaying colorful text in the terminal to checking your system's CPU usage.
Open a Command Prompt or PowerShell window and run the following single command to install all necessary packages at once 1:
Bash
pip install rich psutil requests python-dotenv

Here's what these key libraries do:
rich: A library for creating beautiful and informative terminal outputs. It's responsible for the colors, tables, and progress spinners you'll see.
psutil: A cross-platform library for retrieving information on running processes and system utilization (CPU, memory, disks). This is essential for the agent's self-diagnosis module.
2.3 Setting Up Ollama: Your Local LLM Engine
To avoid expensive API calls and ensure total privacy, DevAgentZero uses Ollama to run LLMs directly on your machine.
Download and Install Ollama:
Go to the official Ollama download page: https://ollama.com/download
Download and run the installer for your operating system.1
Verify Installation:
Once installed, open a new Command Prompt or PowerShell window and type ollama --version. This should display the installed Ollama version, confirming it's ready to use.
2.4 Downloading the Recommended Models
With Ollama installed, you now need to download the "brains" that DevAgentZero will use. For this build, we will primarily use the mistral model, which offers a great balance of performance and size.
Pull the Mistral Model:
In your terminal, run the following command 1:
Bash
ollama run mistral

The first time you run this, Ollama will download the model file (which is several gigabytes). This may take some time depending on your internet connection. Once downloaded, it will start an interactive chat session with the model. You can type /bye to exit.
(Optional) Pull a Code-Specific Model:
For more advanced code generation, you may want to download a model specifically fine-tuned for coding, such as codellama. You can do this with the command:
Bash
ollama run codellama

2.5 Creating the DevAgentZero Project Structure
A well-organized folder structure is essential for a complex project. Before we write any code, we'll create all the necessary directories.
Create the Root Folder:
Open your terminal and navigate to the location where you want to store the project (e.g., your C: drive).
Run: mkdir DevAgentZero
Run: cd DevAgentZero
Create Subdirectories:
From inside the DevAgentZero folder, run the following command to create all the subdirectories the agent will need for its core logic, logs, memory, and outputs 1:
Bash
mkdir agent_core logs memory_store outputs backups

Your workshop is now fully prepared. You have Python, the necessary libraries, a local LLM engine with a powerful model, and a clean folder structure. In the next chapter, we will begin construction by building the agent's "immune system."
Chapter 3: The Guardian at the Gate: Building the Preflight Integrity Engine
Prevailing agentic AI frameworks operate with an implicit assumption of a perfect environment. They are "fair-weather" systems, functionally brilliant under ideal conditions but notoriously fragile when faced with the slightest real-world disruption.1 DevAgentZero is engineered to be different. It is designed to be a resilient, production-grade platform. The first system we will build is its "immune system": the Preflight Integrity Engine.
This system acts as a guardian, performing a mandatory, non-negotiable startup sequence called the Preflight Integrity Check before the agent attempts any complex task.1 This ensures the agent is healthy, its tools are in place, and its environment is stable. This sequence of validation and self-repair is what makes the agent trustworthy.
The resilience of this system is not based on a single script, but on a chain of dependent modules that work together. The agent first creates a record of its perfect state (a manifest), then creates safety copies of its files (backups). Only then can it validate its current state against the record and use the backups to heal itself if something is wrong. This architectural pattern is the core of the agent's ability to self-preserve.
3.1 The System Health Monitor (system_diagnostics.py)
The first step in self-awareness is understanding one's environment. This module gives the agent the ability to check the health of the computer it's running on, specifically the CPU, RAM, and disk space. This information is used later to decide if the system is healthy enough to perform demanding tasks.1
File Location: agent_core/system_diagnostics.py
Full Code:
Python
# File: system_diagnostics.py
# Location: agent_core
# Developer: Craig & DevAgentZero
# Version: 1.1.0
# Last Modified: 2025-07-18
# Purpose: Check local system health including RAM, disk space, and CPU load.
# Notes: Hardened, emoji-free, and ready for CLI or internal integration.

import psutil
from rich.console import Console

console = Console()

MIN_FREE_DISK_GB = 5       # Minimum recommended disk space in GB
MIN_FREE_RAM_MB = 1024     # Minimum recommended free RAM in MB

def check_disk():
"""Checks for available disk space."""
try:
disk = psutil.disk_usage('/')
free_gb = disk.free / (1024 ** 3)
if free_gb < MIN_FREE_DISK_GB:
console.print(f"[system_diagnostics] Low disk space: {free_gb:.2f} GB available")
else:
console.print(f"[system_diagnostics] Disk space OK: {free_gb:.2f} GB available")
return free_gb
except Exception as e:
console.print(f"[system_diagnostics] Error checking disk: {e}")
return 0

def check_ram():
"""Checks for available RAM."""
try:
mem = psutil.virtual_memory()
free_mb = mem.available / (1024 ** 2)
if free_mb < MIN_FREE_RAM_MB:
console.print(f"[system_diagnostics] Low available RAM: {free_mb:.0f} MB")
else:
console.print(f"[system_diagnostics] RAM OK: {free_mb:.0f} MB available")
return free_mb
except Exception as e:
console.print(f"[system_diagnostics] Error checking RAM: {e}")
return 0

def check_cpu():
"""Checks the current CPU load."""
try:
# getloadavg() is more suitable for Unix-like systems
if hasattr(psutil, "getloadavg"):
load = psutil.getloadavg() # 1-minute average
else:
# cpu_percent is a good cross-platform fallback
load = psutil.cpu_percent(interval=1)
console.print(f"[system_diagnostics] CPU load: {load:.2f}%")
return load
except Exception as e:
console.print(f"[system_diagnostics] Error checking CPU: {e}")
return 100.0

def run_diagnostics():
"""Runs all health checks and returns a readiness score from 0 to 100."""
console.print("[system_diagnostics] Starting system health check...")
free_disk = check_disk()
free_ram = check_ram()
cpu_load = check_cpu()

score = 100
if free_disk < MIN_FREE_DISK_GB:
score -= 30
if free_ram < MIN_FREE_RAM_MB:
score -= 30
if cpu_load > 80.0:
score -= 40

console.print(f"[system_diagnostics] System Readiness Score: {score}/100")
console.print("[system_diagnostics] Health check complete.\n")
return score

if __name__ == "__main__":
run_diagnostics()

Code Explanation:
Imports: We import psutil to access system information and rich.console for formatted output.
Constants: MIN_FREE_DISK_GB and MIN_FREE_RAM_MB set the health thresholds.
check_disk(), check_ram(), check_cpu(): Each function uses psutil to get a specific metric (disk usage, virtual memory, CPU load) and prints a status message. They are wrapped in try...except blocks to prevent the agent from crashing if it can't read a metric.
run_diagnostics(): This is the main function. It calls all the individual check functions and calculates a simple "Readiness Score." A low score indicates that the system is under stress, and the agent may choose to defer heavy tasks.
3.2 The Master Checklist (preflight_check.py)
This module is the conductor of the entire self-healing orchestra. It runs on startup and calls all the other validation, backup, and repair modules in the correct sequence.
File Location: preflight_check.py
Full Code:
Python
# File: preflight_check.py
# Location: root
# Developer: Craig & DevAgentZero
# Version: 1.6.0
# Last Modified: 2025-07-19
# Purpose: Complete system bootstrap and repair tool for DevAgentZero with full validation, self-repair, toolchain checks, memory archiving, source import scan, LLM status, and pointer prep.

import subprocess
import importlib.util
from pathlib import Path
from rich.console import Console
from rich.prompt import Prompt
import psutil
import sys
import os
import datetime

# Attempt to import other agent modules, handle gracefully if they don't exist yet
try:
from agent_core.system_diagnostics import run_diagnostics
from log_auditor import audit_session_logs
from backup_manager import backup_critical_files
from version_validator import validate_files
from restore_manager import restore_from_manifest
from manifest_generator import scan_files, save_manifest
from memory_archiver import archive_old_logs
except ImportError as e:
print(f" A core module is missing: {e}. Some checks will be skipped.")
# Define dummy functions so the script can run without all modules present
def run_diagnostics(): print(" Skipping diagnostics.")
def audit_session_logs(): print(" Skipping log audit.")
def backup_critical_files(): print(" Skipping backups.")
def validate_files(): print(" Skipping validation.")
def restore_from_manifest(dry_run=False): print(" Skipping restore.")
def scan_files(): print(" Skipping file scan."); return {}
def save_manifest(manifest): print(" Skipping manifest save.")
def archive_old_logs(): print(" Skipping memory archive.")

console = Console()

REQUIRED_FOLDERS = ["outputs", "logs", "memory_store", "agent_core", "backups"]
REQUIRED_FILES = {
"main.py": "# DevAgentZero main entry point\n",
"agent_core/planner.py": "# Planner module\n",
"agent_core/generator.py": "# Code generator module\n",
"agent_core/executor.py": "# Task executor module\n",
}
REQUIREMENTS_PATH = Path("requirements.txt")

def check_folders():
console.print("\n[bold cyan]Checking Required Folders...[/bold cyan]")
for folder in REQUIRED_FOLDERS:
path = Path(folder)
if not path.exists():
console.print(f"[yellow]Missing folder: {folder}. Creating...[/yellow]")
path.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
else:
console.print(f"[green]✓ Found folder:[/green] {folder}")

def check_files():
console.print("\n[bold cyan]Checking Required Files...[/bold cyan]")
for file, placeholder in REQUIRED_FILES.items():
path = Path(file)
if not path.exists():
console.print(f"[yellow]Missing file: {file}. Creating placeholder...[/yellow]")
path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
path.write_text(placeholder, encoding="utf-8")
else:
console.print(f"[green]✓ Found file:[/green] {file}")

def check_dependencies():
console.print("\n[bold cyan]Checking Python Dependencies...[/bold cyan]")
if not REQUIREMENTS_PATH.exists():
console.print(f"[yellow]'{REQUIREMENTS_PATH}' not found. Skipping dependency check.[/yellow]")
return

try:
with open(REQUIREMENTS_PATH, "r") as f:
reqs = [line.strip().split('==') for line in f if line.strip() and not line.startswith('#')]

missing =
for package in reqs:
if importlib.util.find_spec(package) is None:
missing.append(package)

if missing:
console.print(f"[yellow]Missing packages:[/yellow] {', '.join(missing)}")
if Prompt.ask(f"Install missing packages now?", choices=["y", "n"], default="y") == 'y':
subprocess.check_call([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", *missing])
else:
console.print("[green]✓ All required packages are installed.[/green]")

except Exception as e:
console.print(f"[red]Error checking dependencies: {e}[/red]")

def check_ollama_and_models():
console.print("\n[bold cyan]Checking Ollama and Models...[/bold cyan]")
try:
result = subprocess.run(["ollama", "list"], capture_output=True, text=True, check=False)
if result.returncode!= 0:
console.print("[red]✗ Ollama is not installed or not responding.[/red]")
return

console.print("[green]✓ Ollama is responding.[/green]")
if "mistral" not in result.stdout:
console.print("[yellow]Warning: 'mistral' model not found. Some functions may be limited.[/yellow]")
console.print("[dim]You can install it by running: ollama pull mistral[/dim]")
else:
console.print("[green]✓ Found 'mistral' model.[/green]")
except FileNotFoundError:
console.print("[red]✗ Ollama command not found. Please install Ollama.[/red]")
except Exception as e:
console.print(f"[red]Error checking Ollama: {e}[/red]")

def run_preflight():
console.print("\n[bold magenta]Running DevAgentZero Preflight Check...[/bold magenta]\n")
check_folders()
check_files()
check_dependencies()
check_ollama_and_models()

console.print("\n[bold cyan]Running System Diagnostics...[/bold cyan]")
run_diagnostics()

console.print("\n[bold cyan]Running Maintenance and Integrity Checks...[/bold cyan]")
backup_critical_files()
manifest = scan_files()
save_manifest(manifest)
validate_files()
audit_session_logs()
archive_old_logs()

console.print("\n[bold green]Preflight complete. System is ready.[/bold green]\n")

if __name__ == "__main__":
run_preflight()

Code Explanation:
Graceful Imports: The script uses a try...except ImportError block at the top. This is a clever design that allows preflight_check.py to run even if you haven't created all the other modules yet. It defines dummy functions so the script doesn't crash, making the build process smoother.
check_folders() & check_files(): These functions iterate through lists of required directories and files. If any are missing, they are created automatically. This makes the agent self-healing from accidental deletions.
check_dependencies(): This function reads a requirements.txt file (which you will create later) and checks if all necessary Python packages are installed. If not, it interactively prompts the user to install them.
check_ollama_and_models(): This uses the subprocess module to run the ollama list command. It verifies that Ollama is installed and that the required mistral model is available.
run_preflight(): This is the main function that calls all the individual checks and maintenance tasks in a logical order. It ensures that the foundational checks pass before moving on to more complex tasks like backups and validation.
3.3 The Integrity Ledger (manifest_generator.py & version_validator.py)
For an agent to know if it has been damaged, it must first have a perfect picture of its healthy state. The manifest_generator.py module creates this picture, and version_validator.py uses it to diagnose problems.1
manifest_generator.py
This script scans all critical files in the project and records their metadata—path, size, modification date, and most importantly, a unique cryptographic "fingerprint" called a SHA256 checksum—into a single file named manifest.json.
File Location: manifest_generator.py
Full Code:
Python
# File: manifest_generator.py
# Location: root
# Developer: Craig & DevAgentZero
# Version: 0.2.0
# Last Modified: 2025-07-18
# Purpose: Generate manifest.json with metadata for all.py and.json files for validation, repair, and audit tracking.

import json
import hashlib
from pathlib import Path
from datetime import datetime
from rich.console import Console

console = Console()

MANIFEST_PATH = Path("manifest.json")
# Define what to include in the manifest
TARGET_DIRS = [".", "agent_core"]
TRACKED_EXTENSIONS = [".py", ".json"]

def compute_checksum(file_path):
"""Compute SHA-256 hash of a file for version validation."""
hash_func = hashlib.sha256()
try:
with open(file_path, "rb") as f:
while chunk := f.read(8192):
hash_func.update(chunk)
return hash_func.hexdigest()
except Exception as e:
console.print(f"[red]Error computing checksum for {file_path}: {e}[/red]")
return None

def scan_files():
"""Scan target files and collect structured metadata for the manifest."""
manifest_data = {
"generated_at": datetime.now().isoformat(),
"files":
}

console.print("[manifest_generator] Scanning files to generate manifest...")
for folder in TARGET_DIRS:
for file_path in Path(folder).rglob("*"):
if file_path.is_file() and file_path.suffix in TRACKED_EXTENSIONS:
checksum = compute_checksum(file_path)
if checksum:
metadata = {
"path": str(file_path.relative_to(Path("."))),
"checksum": checksum,
"modified_time": file_path.stat().st_mtime,
"size_bytes": file_path.stat().st_size
}
manifest_data["files"].append(metadata)

return manifest_data

def save_manifest(manifest):
"""Write the manifest data to manifest.json."""
try:
with open(MANIFEST_PATH, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
json.dump(manifest, f, indent=2)
console.print(f"[green]✓ Manifest generated and saved:[/green] {MANIFEST_PATH}")
except Exception as e:
console.print(f"[red]Failed to write manifest.json: {e}[/red]")

if __name__ == "__main__":
manifest = scan_files()
save_manifest(manifest)

Code Explanation:
compute_checksum(): This function reads a file in binary mode and calculates its SHA256 hash. Any change to the file, even a single character, will result in a completely different hash.
scan_files(): This function walks through the specified directories (. for the root and agent_core), finds all files with .py or .json extensions, and collects their metadata, including the checksum.
save_manifest(): This simply writes the collected data into the manifest.json file in a human-readable format.
version_validator.py
This script is the auditor. It reads manifest.json and compares the recorded checksum for each file against a newly calculated checksum of the file on disk. If they don't match, it flags the file for repair.
File Location: version_validator.py
Full Code:
Python
# File: version_validator.py
# Location: root
# Developer: Craig & DevAgentZero
# Version: 0.2.0
# Last Modified: 2025-07-18
# Purpose: Validate current DevAgent Zero files against manifest and trigger repair if mismatched.

import hashlib
import json
from pathlib import Path
from rich.console import Console

# Graceful import for restore_manager
try:
from restore_manager import restore_file
except ImportError:
def restore_file(path, reason, dry_run):
console.print(f" restore_manager not found. Cannot repair {path}.")
return False

MANIFEST_PATH = Path("manifest.json")
console = Console()

def compute_checksum(path: Path) -> str:
"""Computes the SHA-256 checksum of a file."""
hash_func = hashlib.sha256()
with open(path, "rb") as f:
while chunk := f.read(8192):
hash_func.update(chunk)
return hash_func.hexdigest()

def load_manifest():
"""Loads the manifest.json file."""
if not MANIFEST_PATH.exists():
console.print("[red]Manifest file missing. Run manifest_generator.py first.[/red]")
return None
try:
with open(MANIFEST_PATH, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
return json.load(f)
except Exception as e:
console.print(f"[red]Failed to load manifest: {e}[/red]")
return None

def validate_files(dry_run=False):
"""Compares files on disk against the manifest and flags discrepancies."""
manifest = load_manifest()
if not manifest:
return

console.print("[version_validator] Validating file integrity against manifest...")
all_ok = True
for entry in manifest.get("files",):
path = Path(entry["path"])
expected_hash = entry["checksum"]
reason = None

if not path.exists():
reason = "missing"
all_ok = False
else:
try:
current_hash = compute_checksum(path)
if current_hash!= expected_hash:
reason = "hash mismatch"
all_ok = False
except Exception:
reason = "corrupt/unreadable"
all_ok = False

if reason:
console.print(f"[yellow]✗ Validation failed for {path} (Reason: {reason})[/yellow]")
if not dry_run:
restore_file(path, reason=reason, dry_run=dry_run)
else:
console.print(f"[green]✓ OK:[/green] {path}")

if all_ok:
console.print("[green]All files passed integrity check.[/green]")

if __name__ == "__main__":
validate_files()

Code Explanation:
load_manifest(): Safely loads the manifest.json file.
validate_files(): This is the core logic. It iterates through each file listed in the manifest. For each file, it checks if it exists and then calculates its current checksum. If the file is missing or the checksums do not match, it identifies a problem and calls the restore_file function (from the next module we will build) to initiate a repair.
3.4 The Safety Net (backup_manager.py & restore_manager.py)
Validation is useless without a way to fix the problems it finds. These two modules provide the safety net: one creates backups, and the other uses them for restoration.
backup_manager.py
This script creates timestamped backups of all critical files and stores them in the /backups directory. It's smart enough to only create a new backup if the source file has actually changed since the last backup was made.
File Location: backup_manager.py
Full Code:
Python
# File: backup_manager.py
# Location: root
# Developer: Craig & DevAgentZero
# Version: 0.2.0
# Last Modified: 2025-07-18
# Purpose: Perform smart conditional backups of DevAgent Zero core files.

from pathlib import Path
import shutil
import hashlib
import datetime
from rich.console import Console

console = Console()

SOURCE_DIRS = [".", "agent_core"]
BACKUP_DIR = Path("backups")
BACKUP_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

CRITICAL_EXTENSIONS = [".py", ".json"]

def compute_checksum(file_path: Path) -> str:
"""Return SHA256 checksum of the file."""
try:
hash_func = hashlib.sha256()
with file_path.open("rb") as f:
for chunk in iter(lambda: f.read(8192), b""):
hash_func.update(chunk)
return hash_func.hexdigest()
except Exception as e:
console.print(f"[backup_manager] Error computing checksum for {file_path}: {e}")
return ""

def needs_backup(src: Path, backup_dir: Path) -> bool:
"""Return True if no backup exists or if the source file has changed."""
try:
src_hash = compute_checksum(src)
if not src_hash: return False

# Find the latest backup for this file
backups = sorted(backup_dir.glob(f"{src.stem}_bak_*{src.suffix}"), reverse=True)
if not backups:
return True # No backup exists yet

latest_backup = backups
backup_hash = compute_checksum(latest_backup)

return src_hash!= backup_hash
except Exception as e:
console.print(f"[backup_manager] Error comparing checksums for {src}: {e}")
return False

def backup_critical_files():
"""Backup all.py and.json files from key folders if they have changed."""
console.print("[backup_manager] Scanning for files to back up...")
for folder in SOURCE_DIRS:
for src_path in Path(folder).rglob("*"):
if src_path.is_file() and src_path.suffix in CRITICAL_EXTENSIONS:
relative_path = src_path.relative_to(Path("."))
backup_path_dir = BACKUP_DIR / relative_path.parent
backup_path_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

if needs_backup(src_path, backup_path_dir):
timestamp = datetime.datetime.now().strftime("%Y%m%d_%H%M%S")
backup_file_path = backup_path_dir / f"{src_path.stem}_bak_{timestamp}{src_path.suffix}"
try:
shutil.copy2(src_path, backup_file_path)
console.print(f"[green]✓ Backed up:[/green] {src_path} → {backup_file_path.name}")
except Exception as e:
console.print(f"[red]Failed to back up {src_path}: {e}[/red]")

if __name__ == "__main__":
backup_critical_files()

Code Explanation:
needs_backup(): This is the efficiency engine. It computes the checksum of the source file and compares it to the checksum of the most recent backup for that file. If they are the same, no backup is needed.
backup_critical_files(): This function scans the project directories. For each critical file, it calls needs_backup(). If a backup is required, it copies the file to the /backups directory with a timestamp in the filename, preserving a version history.
restore_manager.py
This is the paramedic. When version_validator.py finds a problem, it calls this module. The restore_manager finds the most recent valid backup of the corrupted file and copies it back into place, effectively healing the agent.
File Location: restore_manager.py
Full Code:
Python
# File: restore_manager.py
# Location: root
# Developer: Craig & DevAgentZero
# Version: 0.3.0
# Last Modified: 2025-07-18
# Purpose: Restore latest valid backup for missing, corrupt, or mismatched files.

import shutil
from pathlib import Path
from rich.console import Console

console = Console()

BACKUP_DIR = Path("backups")
TARGET_ROOT = Path(".")
RESTORE_LOG = Path("logs/restore.log")

def find_latest_backup(original_path: Path):
"""Finds the most recent backup file for a given original path."""
relative_path = original_path.relative_to(TARGET_ROOT)
backup_search_dir = BACKUP_DIR / relative_path.parent

if not backup_search_dir.exists():
return None

# Find all backups for this file stem and suffix
candidates = sorted(
backup_search_dir.glob(f"{original_path.stem}_bak_*{original_path.suffix}"),
key=lambda f: f.stat().st_mtime,
reverse=True
)
return candidates if candidates else None

def log_restore_event(path: Path, reason: str, source: Path):
"""Logs a restore event to the restore log file."""
try:
RESTORE_LOG.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
with open(RESTORE_LOG, "a", encoding="utf-8") as log:
timestamp = datetime.datetime.now().isoformat()
log.write(f"[{timestamp}] Restored '{path}' from '{source.name}'. Reason: {reason}\n")
except Exception as e:
console.print(f"[restore_manager][yellow]Warning:[/yellow] Failed to write restore log: {e}")

def restore_file(original_path: Path, reason: str = "unknown", dry_run=False) -> bool:
"""Restores a single file from its most recent backup."""
latest_backup = find_latest_backup(original_path)

if not latest_backup:
console.print(f"[red]✗ No backup found for {original_path}. Cannot restore.[/red]")
return False

if dry_run:
console.print(f"[yellow][dry-run][/yellow] Would restore: {original_path} from {latest_backup.name} (Reason: {reason})")
return True

try:
original_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
shutil.copy2(latest_backup, original_path)
log_restore_event(original_path, reason, latest_backup)
console.print(f"[green]✓ Restored {original_path} from {latest_backup.name}[/green]")
return True
except Exception as e:
console.print(f"[red]✗ Failed to restore {original_path}: {e}[/red]")
return False

if __name__ == "__main__":
# Example usage: python restore_manager.py main.py
import sys
if len(sys.argv) > 1:
file_to_restore = Path(sys.argv)
restore_file(file_to_restore, reason="manual restore")
else:
console.print("[dim]Usage: python restore_manager.py [path/to/file_to_restore.py][/dim]")

Code Explanation:
find_latest_backup(): Given the path of a file that needs to be restored, this function searches the /backups directory for all corresponding backup files and returns the one with the most recent modification time.
log_restore_event(): Every time a file is restored, this function writes an entry to logs/restore.log, creating an audit trail of all self-healing actions.
restore_file(): This is the main function. It finds the latest backup and copies it over the corrupted or missing file. The dry_run parameter is a safety feature that allows the system to simulate a restore without actually changing any files.
With these modules in place, DevAgentZero now has a robust immune system. It can catalog its healthy state, create backups, detect damage, and automatically repair itself, making it far more resilient than typical agentic frameworks.
Chapter 4: The Digital Mind: Building the Memory & Personality Core
A truly intelligent agent needs more than just the ability to execute tasks; it needs a memory and a personality. As noted in the DevAgentZero Foundations Series, first-generation AIs suffer from "digital amnesia," forgetting everything the moment a session ends.1 Furthermore, their impersonal, transactional nature makes them feel like sterile tools rather than collaborative partners.1
This chapter focuses on building the "soul" of DevAgentZero: a persistent, long-term memory system and a dynamic, adaptive personality core. This is achieved through a feedback loop where the agent senses the user's emotional state, shapes its response accordingly, archives the interaction for long-term storage, and reflects on these memories to learn and improve its conversational style over time.
4.1 The Personality Governor (personality_core.py)
This module is the heart of the agent's personality. It maintains a persistent profile of the user and the agent's own conversational state. It tracks things like the user's name, their preferred tone (e.g., formal, casual), and the overall mood of the recent conversation.
File Location: personality_core.py
Full Code:
Python
# File: personality_core.py
# Location: root
# Developer: Craig & DevAgentZero
# Version: 1.1.0
# Last Modified: 2025-07-18
# Purpose: Maintain adaptive personality, mood, and memory of user preferences for DevAgentZero.
# Notes: Emoji-free, hardened I/O, safe fallback and logging.

import json
from pathlib import Path
from rich.console import Console
import datetime

console = Console()
PROFILE_PATH = Path("logs/user_profile.json")
TEMP_PERSONA_PATH = Path("logs/temp_persona.json")

DEFAULT_PROFILE = {
"name": "Builder",
"preferred_tone": "professional",
"mood_trend": "neutral",
"skill_level": "intermediate",
"goals":,
"last_interaction_ts": None,
"history":
}

MAX_HISTORY = 100

def load_user_profile():
"""Loads the current user profile, prioritizing a temporary persona if it exists."""
# Check for a temporary override first
if TEMP_PERSONA_PATH.exists():
try:
with open(TEMP_PERSONA_PATH, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
return json.load(f)
except Exception as e:
console.print(f"[personality_core][yellow]Warning:[/yellow] Failed to load temp persona: {e}")

# Load the main profile
if not PROFILE_PATH.exists():
save_user_profile(DEFAULT_PROFILE)
return DEFAULT_PROFILE

try:
with open(PROFILE_PATH, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
return json.load(f)
except (json.JSONDecodeError, IOError) as e:
console.print(f"[personality_core][red]Error:[/red] Failed to load user profile: {e}. Returning default.")
return DEFAULT_PROFILE

def save_user_profile(profile):
"""Saves the main user profile to disk."""
try:
PROFILE_PATH.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
with open(PROFILE_PATH, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
json.dump(profile, f, indent=2)
except Exception as e:
console.print(f"[personality_core][red]Error:[/red] Failed to save user profile: {e}")

def update_user_history(message: str):
"""Adds a message to the user's interaction history."""
profile = load_user_profile()
if "history" not in profile or not isinstance(profile["history"], list):
profile["history"] =

profile["history"].append(message)
if len(profile["history"]) > MAX_HISTORY:
profile["history"] = profile["history"]

profile["last_interaction_ts"] = datetime.datetime.now().isoformat()
save_user_profile(profile)

def infer_mood(message: str) -> str:
"""A simple keyword-based mood inference function."""
lowered = message.lower()
if any(x in lowered for x in ["tired", "overwhelmed", "burnt", "hurts"]):
return "fatigued"
if any(x in lowered for x in ["awesome", "let's go", "pumped", "yes!"]):
return "energized"
if any(x in lowered for x in ["i don't know", "lost", "stuck", "frustrated", "failed"]):
return "frustrated"
if any(x in lowered for x in ["anxious", "worried", "nervous"]):
return "anxious"
if any(x in lowered for x in ["inspired", "hopeful", "motivated"]):
return "motivated"
return "neutral"

def update_mood_trend(latest_msg: str):
"""Updates the mood trend in the user profile based on the latest message."""
profile = load_user_profile()
profile["mood_trend"] = infer_mood(latest_msg)
save_user_profile(profile)

def get_current_tone() -> str:
"""Gets the current preferred tone from the profile."""
profile = load_user_profile()
return profile.get("preferred_tone", "professional")

def get_current_mood() -> str:
"""Gets the current mood trend from the profile."""
profile = load_user_profile()
return profile.get("mood_trend", "neutral")

if __name__ == "__main__":
profile = load_user_profile()
console.print("\n[personality_core] Current DevAgent User Profile")
console.print(profile)

Code Explanation:
PROFILE_PATH & TEMP_PERSONA_PATH: The module defines paths to two JSON files. user_profile.json stores the long-term personality, while temp_persona.json can be used to temporarily override it (e.g., "be more casual for this session").
load_user_profile() & save_user_profile(): These functions handle the reading and writing of the JSON profile file, with error handling to fall back to a default profile if the file is missing or corrupt.
infer_mood(): This is a simple but effective function that scans the user's message for keywords associated with different emotional states and returns a classification like "frustrated" or "energized."
update_mood_trend(): This function calls infer_mood and saves the result to the user profile, keeping a record of the most recent conversational mood.
4.2 The Emotional Sensor (tone_interpreter.py)
This module acts as the agent's real-time emotional sensor. Its job is to listen for explicit commands from the user that request a change in conversational style. For example, if a user says, "Okay, be more professional now," this module will detect that cue and create the temporary persona file that personality_core.py will then use.
File Location: tone_interpreter.py
Full Code:
Python
# File: tone_interpreter.py
# Location: root
# Developer: Craig & DevAgentZero
# Version: 1.1.0
# Last Modified: 2025-07-18
# Purpose: Dynamically interpret tone/mood cues and update DevAgent Zero’s temporary personality overlay.
# Notes: Error-safe, ASCII-only, refactored for production.

import json
from pathlib import Path
from rich.console import Console

TEMP_PERSONA_PATH = Path("logs/temp_persona.json")
console = Console()

# A dictionary mapping tones to keywords that might trigger them
TONE_KEYWORDS = {
"formal": ["formal", "professional", "serious"],
"casual": ["casual", "chill", "relaxed"],
"mentor": ["mentor", "coach", "guide"],
"encouraging": ["cheer me up", "encourage", "be positive"],
"direct": ["be blunt", "tell it like it is", "no sugarcoat"],
}

def detect_tone_shift(user_input: str) -> str or None:
"""Detects if the user is explicitly requesting a tone shift."""
lowered = user_input.lower()
for tone, keywords in TONE_KEYWORDS.items():
if any(keyword in lowered for keyword in keywords):
return tone
return None

def apply_tone_override(tone: str):
"""Creates a temporary persona file to override the default tone."""
try:
TEMP_PERSONA_PATH.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
# We only override the tone, other personality aspects remain default
override_data = {"preferred_tone": tone}
with open(TEMP_PERSONA_PATH, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
json.dump(override_data, f, indent=2)
console.print(f"[tone_interpreter] Personality override set to: {tone.title()}")
except Exception as e:
console.print(f"[tone_interpreter][red]Error:[/red] Failed to write tone override: {e}")

def maybe_override_tone(user_input: str):
"""Checks for a tone shift cue and applies it if found."""
try:
tone = detect_tone_shift(user_input)
if tone:
apply_tone_override(tone)
except Exception as e:
console.print(f"[tone_interpreter][red]Error:[/red] Error during tone check: {e}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
console.print("[tone_interpreter] Interactive test mode. Type 'exit' to quit.")
while True:
try:
test_input = input("User says > ")
if test_input.lower() == 'exit':
break
maybe_override_tone(test_input)
except KeyboardInterrupt:
break

Code Explanation:
TONE_KEYWORDS: This dictionary is the core of the detection logic. It maps personality styles (like "formal") to a list of keywords a user might say to request that style.
detect_tone_shift(): This function simply checks if any of the keywords are present in the user's input.
apply_tone_override(): If a keyword is detected, this function writes to the temp_persona.json file, setting the preferred_tone to the new value. The main personality_core module is designed to check for this file first, allowing for seamless, temporary changes in behavior.
4.3 The Long-Term Memory Architect (memory_archiver.py & pointer_resolver.py)
To achieve unlimited, persistent memory without slowing the system down with massive log files, DevAgentZero uses an intelligent archival system. Old session logs are compressed, and a small "pointer" file is left in their place, acting like a breadcrumb or a card in a library catalog.
memory_archiver.py
This module acts as the librarian. It periodically scans the memory_store directory for old session logs, compresses them into .gz files to save space, and creates the corresponding pointer file.
File Location: memory_archiver.py
Full Code:
Python
# File: memory_archiver.py
# Location: root
# Developer: Craig & DevAgentZero
# Version: 1.1.0
# Last Modified: 2025-07-18
# Purpose: Compress old session logs and replace them with lightweight pointer metadata.
# Notes: Includes full error handling for compression, timestamp, and pointer creation.

import gzip
import json
from pathlib import Path
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
from rich.console import Console

console = Console()

MEMORY_DIR = Path("memory_store")
ARCHIVE_AFTER_DAYS = 7 # Archive logs older than one week

def compress_json(file_path: Path):
"""Compresses a JSON file using gzip and deletes the original."""
compressed_path = file_path.with_suffix(".json.gz")
try:
with open(file_path, "rb") as f_in, gzip.open(compressed_path, "wb") as f_out:
shutil.copyfileobj(f_in, f_out)
file_path.unlink()
console.print(f"[memory_archiver] Archived: {file_path.name} → {compressed_path.name}")
return compressed_path
except Exception as e:
console.print(f"[memory_archiver][red]Error:[/red] Failed to compress {file_path.name}: {e}")
return None

def create_pointer(original_path: Path, compressed_path: Path):
"""Creates a.pointer file with metadata about the archived session."""
pointer_path = original_path.with_suffix(".pointer")
try:
pointer_data = {
"session_id": original_path.stem.replace("session_", ""),
"archived_file": compressed_path.name,
"archived_at_ts": datetime.now().isoformat()
}
with open(pointer_path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
json.dump(pointer_data, f, indent=2)
console.print(f"[memory_archiver] Pointer created: {pointer_path.name}")
except Exception as e:
console.print(f"[memory_archiver][red]Error:[/red] Failed to create pointer for {original_path.name}: {e}")

def archive_old_logs():
"""Scans for and archives session logs older than the cutoff."""
if not MEMORY_DIR.exists():
console.print("[memory_archiver][yellow]Warning:[/yellow] memory_store folder not found.")
return

cutoff_date = datetime.now() - timedelta(days=ARCHIVE_AFTER_DAYS)
console.print(f"[memory_archiver] Archiving logs older than {cutoff_date.date()}...")

for file in MEMORY_DIR.glob("session_*.json"):
try:
mod_time = datetime.fromtimestamp(file.stat().st_mtime)
if mod_time < cutoff_date:
compressed_file = compress_json(file)
if compressed_file:
create_pointer(file, compressed_file)
except Exception as e:
console.print(f"[memory_archiver][yellow]Warning:[/yellow] Skipped {file.name} due to error: {e}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
import shutil
archive_old_logs()

Code Explanation:
compress_json(): Takes a file path, reads the file, writes its contents to a new gzipped file (.json.gz), and then deletes the original.
create_pointer(): Creates a new file with a .pointer extension. This small JSON file contains the original session ID and the path to the compressed archive file.
archive_old_logs(): This function iterates through all session_*.json files in the memory directory. If a file's modification date is older than the ARCHIVE_AFTER_DAYS threshold, it triggers the compression and pointer creation process.
pointer_resolver.py
This module is responsible for "rehydrating" memories. When the agent needs to access an old session, this script finds the relevant pointer file, uses the information within it to locate and decompress the archive, and restores the full session log.
File Location: pointer_resolver.py
Full Code:
Python
# File: pointer_resolver.py
# Location: root
# Developer: Craig & DevAgentZero
# Version: 1.1.0
# Last Modified: 2025-07-18
# Purpose: Reactivate archived memory sessions from pointer files.
# Notes: Hardened for errors, gzip safety, and clean ASCII logs.

import json
import gzip
from pathlib import Path
from rich.console import Console

console = Console()
MEMORY_DIR = Path("memory_store")

def find_pointer_by_session_id(session_id: str):
"""Finds and loads a pointer file by its session ID."""
pointer_file = MEMORY_DIR / f"session_{session_id}.pointer"
if not pointer_file.exists():
return None
try:
with open(pointer_file, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
return json.load(f)
except Exception as e:
console.print(f"[pointer_resolver][red]Error:[/red] Failed to load pointer file: {e}")
return None

def rehydrate_session(pointer: dict):
"""Decompresses an archived session log and restores it."""
try:
archive_file = MEMORY_DIR / pointer["archived_file"]
if not archive_file.exists():
console.print(f"[pointer_resolver][red]Error:[/red] Archive file missing: {archive_file.name}")
return None

# Restore to a temporary file to avoid overwriting anything
output_path = MEMORY_DIR / f"restored_{pointer['session_id']}.json"
with gzip.open(archive_file, "rb") as f_in, open(output_path, "wb") as f_out:
shutil.copyfileobj(f_in, f_out)

console.print(f"[pointer_resolver] Session restored to: {output_path.name}")
return output_path
except Exception as e:
console.print(f"[pointer_resolver][red]Error:[/red] Failed to rehydrate session: {e}")
return None

def scan_for_reference(text: str):
"""Scans user input for references to archived session IDs."""
try:
# A simple check for the session ID format
if "session_" in text:
for pointer_file in MEMORY_DIR.glob("session_*.pointer"):
session_id = pointer_file.stem.replace("session_", "")
if session_id in text:
console.print(f"[pointer_resolver] Found reference to archived session: {session_id}")
pointer = find_pointer_by_session_id(session_id)
if pointer:
return rehydrate_session(pointer)
except Exception as e:
console.print(f"[pointer_resolver][red]Error:[/red] Error scanning for reference: {e}")
return None

if __name__ == "__main__":
import shutil
sid = input("Enter session ID to restore (e.g., 20250714_143500): ").strip()
pointer = find_pointer_by_session_id(sid)
if pointer:
rehydrate_session(pointer)
else:
console.print("No pointer found for that session ID.")

Code Explanation:
rehydrate_session(): This is the core function. It takes a loaded pointer dictionary, finds the compressed .gz file, and uses the gzip library to decompress it back into a readable .json file.
scan_for_reference(): This function allows the agent to automatically recall memories. It scans the user's input for text that looks like a session ID. If it finds one, it automatically triggers the rehydration process.
4.4 The Learning Engine (reflection_engine.py)
Storing data is not the same as learning. The reflection engine is what allows DevAgentZero to analyze its memory and improve itself. During idle cycles, this module reviews past interactions to identify patterns and optimize its future behavior.
File Location: reflection_engine.py
Full Code:
Python
# File: reflection_engine.py
# Location: root
# Developer: Craig & DevAgentZero
# Version: 1.1.0
# Last Modified: 2025-07-18
# Purpose: Analyze user feedback to adjust DevAgent Zero's tone strategy over time.
# Notes: Hardened with error handling, JSON fallback, and ASCII-safe logging.

import json
from pathlib import Path
from rich.console import Console

TONE_PROFILE = Path("logs/tone_profile.json")
console = Console()

# Keywords to identify positive and negative feedback
POSITIVE_MARKERS = ["thanks", "that helped", "finally worked", "perfect", "awesome", "great"]
FRUSTRATION_MARKERS = ["ugh", "not working", "again?", "come on", "this sucks", "failed"]

def load_tone_profile():
"""Loads the long-term tone profile from disk."""
if not TONE_PROFILE.exists():
return {"confidence": 0, "clarity_bias": 0}
try:
with open(TONE_PROFILE, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
return json.load(f)
except Exception:
# If file is corrupt, start fresh
return {"confidence": 0, "clarity_bias": 0}

def save_tone_profile(profile):
"""Saves the tone profile back to disk."""
try:
TONE_PROFILE.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
with open(TONE_PROFILE, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
json.dump(profile, f, indent=2)
except Exception as e:
console.print(f"[reflection_engine][red]Error:[/red] Failed to save tone profile: {e}")

def analyze_feedback(user_input: str):
"""Analyzes user input for feedback cues and updates the tone profile."""
try:
profile = load_tone_profile()
lowered = user_input.strip().lower()
adjusted = False

if any(word in lowered for word in POSITIVE_MARKERS):
profile["confidence"] = profile.get("confidence", 0) + 1
adjusted = True

if any(word in lowered for word in FRUSTRATION_MARKERS):
profile["clarity_bias"] = profile.get("clarity_bias", 0) + 1
adjusted = True

if adjusted:
save_tone_profile(profile)
console.print("[reflection_engine] Tone profile updated based on feedback.")
except Exception as e:
console.print(f"[reflection_engine][red]Error:[/red] Error analyzing feedback: {e}")

def get_tone_strategy():
"""Suggests a conversational strategy based on the long-term profile."""
profile = load_tone_profile()
strategy =
if profile.get("confidence", 0) > 5:
strategy.append("Be more encouraging.")
if profile.get("clarity_bias", 0) > 3:
strategy.append("Be more direct and clear.")
return strategy if strategy else ["Maintain neutral tone."]

if __name__ == "__main__":
console.print(f"Current tone strategy: {get_tone_strategy()}")

Code Explanation:
TONE_PROFILE: This module maintains its own persistent log, tone_profile.json, which stores long-term metrics about what kind of responses work best for the user.
analyze_feedback(): This function is called after the agent responds to the user. It scans the user's next message for keywords. If the user says something positive ("thanks, that worked!"), it increments a "confidence" score. If they say something negative ("ugh, it failed again"), it increments a "clarity_bias" score.
get_tone_strategy(): This function reads the scores from the profile. In a more advanced implementation, these scores would directly influence the response templates chosen by personality_core.py. For example, a high "clarity_bias" score might tell the agent to use shorter sentences and provide more explicit instructions in the future.
This complete feedback loop—sensing mood, shaping a response, and then reflecting on the outcome—is what allows DevAgentZero to evolve from a generic tool into a truly personalized and intelligent partner.
Chapter 5: The Application Factory: Building the Agentic Loop
This chapter is where we build the engine of DevAgentZero—the "Application Factory." This is the core agentic loop responsible for taking a user's request, creating a plan, generating code, and executing the result. As described in Volume I – Autonomous Agent Infrastructure, this is the system that turns high-level goals into tangible, working software.1 It is a sequence of specialized modules, each with a single job, working together like an assembly line.
5.1 The Model Router (model_manager.py)
Not all LLMs are created equal. Some are better at conversation, while others excel at writing code. The Model Manager is a simple but crucial utility that allows the agent to select the best local model for the task at hand. For now, it will be hardcoded, but this module makes it easy to add more complex logic in the future.
File Location: model_manager.py
Full Code:
Python
# File: model_manager.py
# Location: root
# Developer: Craig & DevAgentZero
# Version: 1.1.0
# Last Modified: 2025-07-18
# Purpose: Provide dynamic model selection, availability checks, and routing for DevAgent Zero tasks.
# Notes: Fully ASCII-safe and error-tolerant.

import subprocess
from rich.console import Console

console = Console()

# Define model metadata and their preferred use cases
MODELS = {
"mistral": {
"description": "Fast 7B model good for code and light reasoning.",
"preferred_tasks": ["plan", "code", "execute", "chat", "fallback"],
},
"codellama": {
"description": "Specialized model for high-quality code generation.",
"preferred_tasks": ["code"],
},
"openhermes": {
"description": "Fine-tuned model for better chat tone.",
"preferred_tasks": ["chat", "conversation"],
}
}

def check_model_available(name: str) -> bool:
"""Checks if a specific Ollama model is installed locally."""
try:
result = subprocess.run(["ollama", "list"], capture_output=True, text=True, check=False)
return name.lower() in result.stdout.lower()
except Exception as e:
console.print(f"[model_manager][red]Error:[/red] Error checking model availability: {e}")
return False

def get_best_model(task_type: str) -> str:
"""Selects the best available model for a given task type."""
try:
# Try to find an ideal model that is installed
for name, meta in MODELS.items():
if task_type in meta["preferred_tasks"]:
if check_model_available(name):
console.print(f"[model_manager] Optimal model for '{task_type}': {name}")
return name

# If no ideal model is found, use the default fallback
console.print(f"[model_manager][yellow]Warning:[/yellow] No optimal model for '{task_type}' found. Using default.")
return "mistral"
except Exception as e:
console.print(f"[model_manager][red]Error:[/red] Failed during model selection: {e}")
return "mistral" # Fallback on any error

if __name__ == "__main__":
console.print("\n[model_manager] Available Model Profiles:")
for name, meta in MODELS.items():
status = "[green]AVAILABLE[/green]" if check_model_available(name) else "[red]MISSING[/red]"
console.print(f"{status:<19} {name:<12} - {meta['description']}")

Code Explanation:
MODELS Dictionary: This defines the "known" models and maps them to the types of tasks they are good at. For example, codellama is listed as preferred for the "code" task.
check_model_available(): This function runs ollama list to see which models are actually installed on the user's machine.
get_best_model(): This is the main function. It takes a task_type (e.g., "plan") and searches the MODELS dictionary for the best-suited model that is also currently available. If it can't find a perfect match, it defaults to mistral.
5.2 The Blueprint Creator (planner.py)
This is the architect of the agentic loop. It takes the user's high-level goal (e.g., "build a web scraper") and uses an LLM to break it down into a logical, step-by-step plan that the other modules can execute.
File Location: agent_core/planner.py
Full Code:
Python
# File: planner.py
# Location: agent_core
# Developer: Craig & DevAgentZero
# Version: 1.1.0
# Last Modified: 2025-07-18
# Purpose: Generate step-by-step development plans using the best-fit LLM model.
# Notes: Hardened against timeout, stream-safe, emoji-free.

import subprocess
import time
from rich.console import Console
from model_manager import get_best_model

console = Console()
OLLAMA_TIMEOUT = 60 # seconds

def plan_tasks(goal: str) -> list:
"""Generates a multi-step plan to achieve a given goal."""

prompt = f"""You are an expert software architect. Your job is to take a high-level goal and break it down into a clear, numbered list of 3-6 actionable steps for an AI developer agent.

Goal: "{goal}"

Only output the numbered list of steps. Do not include any explanation, commentary, or markdown formatting.
Example:
1. Step one.
2. Step two.
3. Step three.
"""

console.print("[planner] Thinking about the request to generate a plan...")
model = get_best_model("plan")

try:
console.print(f"[planner] Calling model '{model}' to generate plan...")
result = subprocess.run(
["ollama", "run", model],
input=prompt,
capture_output=True,
text=True,
timeout=OLLAMA_TIMEOUT
)

if result.returncode!= 0:
console.print(f"[planner][red]Error:[/red] Ollama returned an error: {result.stderr.strip()}")
return fallback_plan(goal)

response = result.stdout.strip()
if not response:
raise ValueError("Ollama returned an empty response.")

# Clean up the response to get a list of steps
steps = [line.strip("-•1234567890. ").strip() for line in response.splitlines() if line.strip()]

if not steps:
console.print("[planner][yellow]Warning:[/yellow] Could not parse steps from model output.")
return fallback_plan(goal)

return steps

except (subprocess.TimeoutExpired, ValueError) as e:
console.print(f"[planner][red]Error:[/red] {e}. Using fallback plan generator.")
return fallback_plan(goal)
except Exception as e:
console.print(f"[planner][red]Error:[/red] An unexpected error occurred: {e}")
return fallback_plan(goal)

def fallback_plan(goal: str) -> list:
"""A simple, generic plan to use when the LLM fails."""
return

if __name__ == "__main__":
test_goal = "Build a script that checks disk space and CPU load"
plan = plan_tasks(test_goal)
console.print("\n[bold]Generated Plan:[/bold]")
for i, step in enumerate(plan, 1):
print(f"{i}. {step}")

Code Explanation:
plan_tasks(): This function constructs a detailed prompt for the LLM. This is a key part of "prompt engineering"—it tells the model exactly what its role is ("expert software architect") and the exact format for the output (a numbered list).
Model Selection: It calls get_best_model("plan") to select the right tool for the job.
Subprocess Call: It uses subprocess.run to send the prompt to the Ollama model. It includes a timeout to prevent the agent from hanging indefinitely if the model is unresponsive.
Response Parsing: The raw text output from the LLM is cleaned up to create a simple Python list of strings, where each string is one step of the plan.
fallback_plan(): If the LLM fails for any reason, this function provides a generic, safe plan to prevent the agent from crashing. This is a key resilience pattern.
5.3 The Code Generator (generator.py)
Once the plan is created, this module takes one step at a time and generates the actual Python code needed to accomplish it.
File Location: agent_core/generator.py
Full Code:
Python
# File: generator.py
# Location: agent_core
# Developer: Craig & DevAgentZero
# Version: 1.1.0
# Last Modified: 2025-07-18
# Purpose: Generate Python code for a given task using the best-fit LLM model.
# Notes: Hardened against malformed LLM output; uses fallback templates.

import subprocess
import textwrap
from rich.console import Console
from model_manager import get_best_model

console = Console()

def generate_code(task: str) -> str:
"""Generates a block of Python code to complete a single task."""

system_prompt = textwrap.dedent(f"""
You are an expert Python engineer. Your job is to write a complete, working, and secure Python script for the following task:

Task: "{task}"

Your response must ONLY include the raw Python code. Do not include explanations, markdown fences (```), or any commentary.
Use best practices, include all necessary imports, and ensure the code is ready to be saved to a.py file and run.
""")

model = get_best_model("code")
console.print(f"[generator] Calling model '{model}' for code generation...")

try:
result = subprocess.run(
["ollama", "run", model],
input=system_prompt,
capture_output=True,
text=True,
timeout=120 # Longer timeout for code generation
)

raw_output = result.stdout.strip()

# Basic validation to ensure the output looks like code
if not raw_output or ("import" not in raw_output and "def" not in raw_output and "print" not in raw_output):
raise ValueError("Output does not appear to be valid Python code.")

# Clean markdown fences if the model accidentally includes them
if raw_output.startswith("```python"):
raw_output = raw_output.replace("```python", "").strip()
if raw_output.startswith("```"):
raw_output = raw_output.replace("```", "").strip()

console.print("[generator] Code generation successful.")
return raw_output

except Exception as e:
console.print(f"[generator][red]Error:[/red] {e}")
return fallback_code(task)

def fallback_code(task: str) -> str:
"""A simple fallback to return if code generation fails."""
console.print(f"[generator] Using fallback template for: {task}")
return f'# Task: {task}\nprint("DevAgentZero code generator failed for this task.")\n'

if __name__ == "__main__":
example_task = "Create a script that prints the current date and time."
generated_code = generate_code(example_task)
console.print("\n[bold]Generated Code:[/bold]")
print(generated_code)

Code Explanation:
System Prompt: The prompt here is even more strict than the planner's. It explicitly tells the model "Your response must ONLY include the raw Python code." This is critical to prevent the model from adding conversational text that would cause a syntax error.
Model Selection: It calls get_best_model("code"), which might select a specialized model like codellama if it's available.
Output Cleaning: The code includes logic to strip out common markdown formatting like ```python that models sometimes add, even when instructed not to. This makes the output more reliable.
5.4 The Quality Inspector (test_runner.py)
Before running potentially flawed code, it's wise to perform a quick check. This module acts as a simple quality inspector, attempting to compile the generated code to catch basic syntax errors before the executor tries to run it.
File Location: test_runner.py
Full Code:
Python
# File: test_runner.py
# Location: root
# Developer: Craig & DevAgentZero
# Version: 1.1
# Last Modified: 2025-07-18
# Purpose: Validate Python code syntax by compiling it.
# Notes: Includes error handling for unreadable or corrupt files.

from rich.console import Console
from pathlib import Path

console = Console()

def run_validation(code_string: str, filename: str = "temp_code.py") -> bool:
"""
Attempts to compile a string of Python code to detect syntax errors.
Returns True if valid, False if syntax fails.
"""
try:
compile(code_string, filename, 'exec')
console.print(f"[test_runner][green]✓ Syntax validation passed for {filename}[/green]")
return True
except SyntaxError as e:
console.print(f"[test_runner][red]✗ Syntax validation failed for {filename}: {e}[/red]")
return False
except Exception as e:
console.print(f"[test_runner][red]✗ An unexpected error occurred during validation: {e}[/red]")
return False

if __name__ == "__main__":
valid_code = "import os\nprint('Hello, World!')"
invalid_code = "import os\nprint 'Hello, World!'"

print("--- Testing valid code ---")
run_validation(valid_code)

print("\n--- Testing invalid code ---")
run_validation(invalid_code)

Code Explanation:
compile() function: This is a built-in Python function. It takes a string of source code, a filename, and a mode ('exec' for a full script) and attempts to turn it into Python bytecode. If there's a syntax error (like a missing colon or mismatched parentheses), it will raise a SyntaxError exception.
run_validation(): This function wraps the compile() call in a try...except block. If compile() succeeds, the function returns True. If it fails, it catches the exception, prints an error message, and returns False.
5.5 The Task Executor (executor.py)
This is the "builder" on the assembly line. It takes the validated code, saves it to a .py file in the /outputs directory, and then runs that file using a subprocess, capturing any output or errors.
File Location: agent_core/executor.py
Full Code:
Python
# File: executor.py
# Location: agent_core
# Developer: Craig & DevAgentZero
# Version: 1.1.0
# Last Modified: 2025-07-18
# Purpose: Execute generated code steps and handle runtime testing.
# Notes: Hardened, emoji-free, and uses reflection engine for tone feedback.

from rich.console import Console
from pathlib import Path
import subprocess
import datetime

console = Console()

OUTPUT_DIR = Path("outputs")
OUTPUT_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

def execute_step(code: str, step_name: str, session_id: str) -> (bool, Path):
"""Saves code to a file and executes it, returning success status and file path."""

console.print(f"\n[executor] Executing step: {step_name}")

# Sanitize step_name to create a valid filename
safe_step_name = "".join(c for c in step_name if c.isalnum() or c in (' ', '_')).rstrip()
safe_step_name = safe_step_name.replace(' ', '_')
timestamp = datetime.datetime.now().strftime("%H%M%S")
filename = OUTPUT_DIR / f"{session_id}_{timestamp}_{safe_step_name[:30]}.py"

try:
with open(filename, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
f.write(code)
console.print(f"[executor] Code saved to: {filename.name}")
except IOError as e:
console.print(f"[executor][red]Error:[/red] Failed to write code to file: {e}")
return False, None

try:
console.print(f"[executor] Running script: {filename.name}...")
result = subprocess.run(
[sys.executable, str(filename)],
capture_output=True,
text=True,
timeout=30
)

if result.returncode == 0:
output = result.stdout.strip()
console.print(f"[executor][green]✓ Success.[/green] Output: {output if output else '(no output)'}")
return True, filename
else:
error = result.stderr.strip()
console.print(f"[executor][red]✗ Runtime Error:[/red] {error}")
return False, filename

except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
console.print("[executor][red]✗ Execution timed out.[/red]")
return False, filename
except Exception as e:
console.print(f"[executor][red]✗ Unexpected execution error:[/red] {e}")
return False, filename

if __name__ == "__main__":
import sys
sid = datetime.datetime.now().strftime("%Y%m%d_%H%M%S")
test_code = "import platform\nprint(f'Running on {platform.system()}')"
execute_step(test_code, "Check OS", sid)

Code Explanation:
File Naming: The function generates a unique, descriptive filename for each step, including the session ID, a timestamp, and a sanitized version of the step name. This keeps the /outputs directory organized.
Saving the Code: It writes the code string provided by the generator to the new file.
subprocess.run(): This is the key function for execution. It runs the Python script in a separate process.
sys.executable: This ensures the script is run with the same Python interpreter that is running the agent.
capture_output=True: This tells the subprocess to capture anything the script prints.
text=True: This ensures the output is decoded as text.
timeout=30: A safety measure to kill the script if it runs for too long.
Result Handling: It checks the returncode of the process. A code of 0 means success. Any other code indicates an error, in which case it prints the error message captured from stderr.
5.6 The Central Orchestrator (main.py)
Finally, the main.py script ties everything together. It is the entry point for the entire application. It initializes the agent, runs the all-important preflight check, and then enters the main loop where it interacts with the user and orchestrates the planner, generator, and executor to fulfill build requests.
File Location: main.py
Full Code:
Python
# File: main.py
# Location: root
# Developer: Craig & DevAgentZero
# Version: 2.0.0
# Last Modified: 2025-07-19
# Purpose: Launch DevAgentZero, run preflight, and enter chat or build mode.

from rich.console import Console
import datetime
from pathlib import Path
import json
import sys

# Core Agent Modules
from preflight_check import run_preflight
from agent_core.planner import plan_tasks
from agent_core.generator import generate_code
from test_runner import run_validation
from agent_core.executor import execute_step

# Personality & Memory Modules
from personality_core import update_user_history, update_mood_trend, get_current_mood, get_current_tone
from tone_interpreter import maybe_override_tone
from reflection_engine import analyze_feedback

console = Console()
MEMORY_DIR = Path("memory_store")

def log_session(session_id, prompt, plan, outputs):
"""Logs the entire session to a JSON file."""
log_data = {
"session_id": session_id,
"timestamp": datetime.datetime.now().isoformat(),
"prompt": prompt,
"plan": plan,
"outputs": {str(path): status for path, status in outputs.items()}
}
log_file = MEMORY_DIR / f"session_{session_id}.json"
try:
with open(log_file, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
json.dump(log_data, f, indent=2)
console.print(f"[main] Session log saved to {log_file.name}")
except Exception as e:
console.print(f"[main][red]Error:[/red] Could not save session log: {e}")

def chat_mode():
"""Handles conversational interactions with the agent."""
console.print("\n[bold green]💬 Chat mode active. Ask me anything, or type 'build' to create something or 'exit' to leave.[/bold green]\n")
while True:
try:
user_input = console.input("[bold]You:[/bold] ").strip()
if user_input.lower() == "exit":
break
if user_input.lower() == "build":
build_mode()
# After returning from build mode, re-enter chat prompt
console.print("\n[bold green]💬 Chat mode active. What's next?[/bold green]\n")
continue

# Process input through personality core
update_user_history(user_input)
update_mood_trend(user_input)
maybe_override_tone(user_input)

# Generate a conversational response
mood = get_current_mood()
if mood == "frustrated":
response = "It sounds like things are a bit frustrating right now. How can I help clarify or fix something?"
elif mood == "energized":
response = "Great energy! Let's build something amazing. What's on your mind?"
else:
response = "I'm here to help. You can ask me questions, or type 'build' to start a new project."

console.print(f"[bold]DevAgentZero:[/bold] {response}")
analyze_feedback(user_input) # Reflect on the interaction

except (KeyboardInterrupt, EOFError):
break
except Exception as e:
console.print(f"[main][red]Chat error:[/red] {e}")

def build_mode():
"""Handles the agentic build loop."""
try:
prompt = console.input("\n[bold blue]What would you like to build? > [/bold]").strip()
if not prompt:
console.print("[yellow]Build cancelled.[/yellow]")
return

session_id = datetime.datetime.now().strftime("%Y%m%d_%H%M%S")

plan = plan_tasks(prompt)
if not plan:
console.print("[red]Could not generate a plan. Please try rephrasing your request.[/red]")
return

console.print("\n[bold yellow]Generated Plan:[/bold yellow]")
for i, step in enumerate(plan, 1):
console.print(f"[bold]{i}.[/bold] {step}")

if console.input("\n[bold]Execute this plan? (y/n) > [/bold]").lower()!= "y":
console.print("[red]Execution cancelled by user.[/red]")
return

outputs = {} # To store file paths and their success status
for step in plan:
code = generate_code(step)
if not run_validation(code, filename=f"{step[:20]}.py"):
console.print(f"[red]Syntax validation failed for step: '{step}'. Aborting build.[/red]")
outputs["validation_failed"] = "FAIL"
break

success, file_path = execute_step(code, step, session_id)
if file_path:
outputs[file_path] = "PASS" if success else "FAIL"

if not success:
console.print(f"[red]Execution failed for step: '{step}'. Aborting build.[/red]")
break

log_session(session_id, prompt, plan, outputs)

except (KeyboardInterrupt, EOFError):
console.print("\nBuild interrupted by user.")
except Exception as e:
console.print(f"[main][red]Build mode error:[/red] {e}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
try:
run_preflight()
console.print("[bold cyan]\nGood morning,[/bold cyan] what would you like to do today?")
chat_mode()
console.print("\nDevAgentZero shutting down. Goodbye!")
except (KeyboardInterrupt, EOFError):
console.print("\nDevAgentZero shutdown.")
except Exception as e:
console.print(f"[main][red]Fatal startup error:[/red] {e}")
sys.exit(1)

Code Explanation:
Imports: It imports the primary function from almost every other module we've built, positioning itself as the central controller.
log_session(): After a build is complete (or fails), this function gathers all the information—the initial prompt, the generated plan, and the paths to all output files—and saves it to a single session log in memory_store.
chat_mode() vs. build_mode(): The agent has two primary modes. chat_mode is for general conversation and leverages the personality core. build_mode initiates the plan-generate-execute sequence.
if __name__ == "__main__":: This is the standard Python entry point. When you run python main.py, this is the code that executes. It first calls run_preflight() to ensure the system is healthy, then greets the user and enters the main chat_mode loop.
Chapter 6: First Flight: Testing and Running DevAgentZero
You have meticulously assembled every component of DevAgentZero. The brain, the immune system, and the soul are all in place. Now it's time to bring your creation to life. This chapter will guide you through running the agent for the first time, interacting with it, and verifying that all its systems are functioning correctly.
6.1 Running the Full Preflight Check
Before the main launch, it's good practice to run the preflight check manually to see a detailed report of the agent's health.
Open a new Command Prompt or PowerShell window.
Navigate to your DevAgentZero project directory: cd C:\DevAgentZero
Run the preflight script:
Bash
python preflight_check.py

Interpret the Output: You should see a series of checks for folders, files, dependencies, and Ollama. If everything is set up correctly, you will see green "✓" marks and "OK" statuses. If anything is missing, the script will alert you in yellow or red text and may offer to fix the issue. Ensure all checks pass before proceeding.
6.2 Initiating a Conversation: Chat Mode vs. Build Mode
With a successful preflight check, you are ready for the main launch.
In the same terminal window, run the main script:
Bash
python main.py

You will first see the preflight check run again automatically. This is by design; the agent always ensures it is healthy before interacting.
After the check, you will be greeted with a message like: "Good morning, what would you like to do today?" and a "You:" prompt. The agent has started in Chat Mode.1
Test Chat Mode: Type something conversational, like hello, who are you? The agent should give you a simple, helpful response.
Switch to Build Mode: Now, at the "You:" prompt, simply type build. The agent will recognize this keyword and switch to Build Mode, presenting you with a new prompt: "What would you like to build? >".1
6.3 Your First Build Request: Step-by-Step Execution
Let's give the agent its first simple task to test the entire agentic loop.
At the "What would you like to build?" prompt, type: create a python script that prints hello world and press Enter.
Observe the Agent's Thought Process: You will see a series of status messages in the terminal as the agent works 1:
[planner] Thinking about the request...
[planner] Calling model 'mistral' to generate plan...
A "Generated Plan" will be printed with a few logical steps.
Provide Execution Consent: The agent will ask for your permission before running the plan: Execute this plan? (y/n) >. Type y and press Enter.
Watch the Execution: The agent will now execute each step in the plan, providing real-time feedback:
[generator] Calling model 'mistral' for code generation...
[test_runner] Syntax validation passed...
[executor] Code saved to [filename].py
[executor] Running script...
[executor] ✓ Success. Output: hello world
Session Logging: Finally, the agent will confirm that it has logged the entire interaction: [main] Session log saved to session_[timestamp].json.
6.4 Reviewing the Output: Checking Logs and Generated Files
The agent has completed its task. Now, let's verify the artifacts it created.
Check the Output File:
Open your file explorer and navigate to the DevAgentZero/outputs directory.
You will find the .py file the agent created. Open it with a text editor to see the "hello world" code that the LLM generated.
Check the Memory Log:
Navigate to the DevAgentZero/memory_store directory.
You will find the session_[timestamp].json file. Open it to see the structured record of the entire interaction, including your initial prompt, the agent's plan, and the path to the output file it created.
Congratulations! You have successfully built, launched, and tested your own autonomous AI agent.
Chapter 7: Demo Project: Building a CPU & RAM Monitoring Tool
Now that you've confirmed the agent is working with a simple "Hello, World!" test, let's give it a more complex, real-world task. This project will showcase the agent's ability to generate code that interacts with system libraries, perform file I/O, and run in a continuous loop—a task specifically used during the agent's own development and testing.
7.1 Defining the Goal in Plain English
The key to working with an agentic AI is to provide a clear, concise, and unambiguous goal. We will ask the agent to build a utility script that monitors system resources and logs them to a file.
Launch the agent if it's not already running: python main.py
If you are in chat mode, type build to switch to build mode.
At the "What would you like to build?" prompt, enter the following goal :
Build a script that logs CPU and RAM usage to a CSV file every 10 seconds.

7.2 Engaging DevAgentZero to Plan and Build the Tool
Press Enter and observe the agent as it begins the agentic loop.
Planning Phase: The planner module will engage the mistral model. You will see a plan similar to this appear on your screen:
Generated Plan:
1. Import necessary libraries: psutil, csv, time, and datetime.
2. Define the main function to run the monitoring loop.
3. Create and open a CSV file named 'system_monitor_log.csv' in write mode.
4. Write the header row to the CSV file: 'timestamp', 'cpu_percent', 'ram_percent'.
5. Implement an infinite loop that retrieves CPU and RAM usage every 10 seconds.
6. Write the collected data as a new row to the CSV file.

Execution Phase: When prompted to Execute this plan? (y/n), type y. The agent will now proceed step-by-step. For each step, the generator will create a piece of the final script, the test_runner will validate it, and the executor will save it. In this case, since the plan describes a single script, the agent will likely generate one complete file.
7.3 Running the Final Application
Once the agent completes the build, it will have created a Python script in your outputs folder.
Navigate to the DevAgentZero/outputs directory.
Locate the Python file created during the session (e.g., 20240101_123000_..._log_cpu_and_ram_usage.py).
Run the script from your terminal:
Bash
python outputs/[your_script_name].py

The script will start running and will not exit, as it's in an infinite loop. It will not print anything to the console.
Verify the Output: While the script is running, look inside the outputs directory. You should see a new file named system_monitor_log.csv. Open this file with a text editor or spreadsheet program. You will see the data being written to the file every 10 seconds, with new rows appearing as you watch.
To stop the script, go back to your terminal and press Ctrl+C.
7.4 Reviewing the Session Memory
Every action the agent takes is recorded. Let's review the memory of this build session to see how the agent documented its own work.
From your DevAgentZero root directory, run the memory_reader script:
Bash
python memory_reader.py

This utility will display the most recent session logs. You will see a formatted summary of the CPU monitoring tool build, including:
The session timestamp.
Your original prompt.
The full, multi-step plan the agent generated.
A list of all output files created, including the final Python script.
This demo project validates the entire end-to-end functionality of DevAgentZero. You have successfully used your agent to autonomously plan and build a useful software utility based on a single, high-level English command.

Below is the complete, final directory structure for the DevAgentZero project. This tree represents a healthy, fully built agent with all necessary modules, configuration files, and data directories in their correct locations.1

├── model_manager.py

├── restore_manager.py
├── memory_archiver.py
├── pointer_resolver.py
├── personality_core.py

│

│   ├── executor.py
│   └── system_diagnostics.py
│
├── backups/
│   └── (Contains timestamped backups of core files)
│
├── logs/
│   ├── user_profile.json
│   ├── tone_profile.json
│   ├── restore.log
│   └── (Other runtime logs will appear here)
│
├── memory_store/
│   └── (session_*.json, session_*.pointer, session_*.json.gz files appear here)
│
└── outputs/
└── (Scripts and applications generated by the agent appear here)

Appendix C: Launcher Scripts
To make running DevAgentZero easier, you can use these simple launcher scripts. They automatically navigate to the correct directory and start the agent's main script.
Windows Launcher (Run_DevAgentZero.bat)
Save this file in your DevAgentZero root directory. You can then create a desktop shortcut to it for one-click access.1
Code snippet
@echo off
setlocal

REM === DevAgent Zero Launch Script ===
REM Purpose: Navigates to the agent's directory and starts the main script.

REM Navigate to the directory where this script is located
cd /d "%~dp0"

REM Ensure Python is available
where python >nul 2>&1
if %errorlevel% neq 0 (
echo Python is not installed or not in your system's PATH.
pause
exit /b 1
)

REM Launch the agent
echo [INFO] Starting DevAgent Zero...
python main.py

REM Wait for a key press before closing the window
echo [INFO] DevAgent Zero has exited. Press any key to close this window.
pause
endlocal

Linux/macOS Launcher (run_devagentzero.sh)
Save this file in your DevAgentZero root directory. You will need to make it executable by running chmod +x run_devagentzero.sh in your terminal.1
Bash
#!/bin/bash
# File: run_devagentzero.sh
# Location: root
# Developer: Craig & DevAgentZero
# Version: 1.0.0
# Last Modified: 2025-07-18
# Purpose: Cross-platform launcher for DevAgent Zero on Unix systems (Linux/macOS).

# === DevAgent Zero Launcher (Unix) ===

# Get the directory where the script is located
AGENT_DIR="$( cd "$( dirname "${BASH_SOURCE}" )" &> /dev/null && pwd )"

# Check for Python 3
if! command -v python3 &> /dev/null; then
echo " Python 3 is not installed or not in your PATH."
exit 1
fi

# Navigate to the project directory
cd "$AGENT_DIR" |

| { echo " Failed to enter $AGENT_DIR"; exit 1; }

# Launch agent
echo "[INFO] Launching DevAgent Zero..."
python3 main.py

# Completion notice
echo "[INFO] DevAgent Zero execution complete."

Glossary of Terms
Agentic AI: A type of artificial intelligence that can proactively take steps to achieve a high-level goal, rather than just reacting to direct commands. It can plan, execute, and learn.
Agentic Loop: The core operational cycle of an agentic AI: Think → Plan → Build → Test → Reflect.
Checksum: A unique digital "fingerprint" (often a SHA256 hash) of a file. It is used to verify that a file has not been altered or corrupted.
LLM (Large Language Model): A type of AI trained on vast amounts of text data to understand and generate human-like language. Examples include Mistral and CodeLLaMA.
Local-First: A software design philosophy where the primary functions of an application run directly on the user's machine, without requiring a constant connection to a remote server. This prioritizes privacy, performance, and offline capability.
Manifest: A JSON file (manifest.json) that acts as a ledger or record of all critical files in the DevAgentZero system and their correct checksums.
Ollama: A tool that allows users to easily download and run powerful Large Language Models on their local computers.
Pointer File: A small metadata file (e.g., session_123.pointer) that contains a summary and the location of a larger, compressed memory archive. It acts as a "breadcrumb" for the agent to find old memories.
Preflight Check: A mandatory series of diagnostic and self-healing routines that DevAgentZero runs on startup to ensure its own integrity and the health of its environment before executing any tasks.
Rehydration: The process of taking a compressed memory archive (.json.gz file), decompressing it, and loading it back into a usable format. This is triggered by the pointer_resolver.
Subprocess: A separate program or script that is run by the main application. DevAgentZero uses subprocesses to execute the code it generates, isolating it from the agent's core process.
